title: One in Four Depression Cases May Be Driven by Inflammation — and Standard Antidepressants Often Don't Work for Them
excerpt: Growing evidence points to a distinct subtype of depression fuelled by chronic inflammation, with implications for South Asians who carry higher metabolic and inflammatory risk.
body:
For decades, depression has been treated primarily as a problem of brain chemistry — too little serotonin, not enough dopamine. But a growing body of evidence is complicating that picture, and the implications may be especially relevant for the South Asian diaspora.

According to recent reporting by *The New York Times*, drawing on multiple studies and clinical trials, roughly one in four people with depression have elevated levels of inflammatory proteins circulating in their blood. These individuals tend to experience a specific cluster of symptoms — crushing fatigue, poor sleep, low appetite, and a profound absence of motivation — and they are significantly less likely to respond to the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) that remain the most commonly prescribed antidepressants worldwide.

Researchers are calling this emerging pattern "inflamed depression," and it is forcing a rethink of how the condition is diagnosed and treated.

The Biology Behind Inflamed Depression

The connection between inflammation and mood is not new. Scientists have known for years that patients with autoimmune diseases, chronic infections, and metabolic syndrome experience depression at higher rates than the general population. What is new is the growing recognition that inflammation may not merely accompany depression — it may actively drive it.

Dr. David Goldsmith, an associate professor of psychiatry at Emory University School of Medicine, explained to the *Times* that inflammatory proteins can interfere with the brain chemicals that regulate mood and motivation. They disrupt serotonin and dopamine signalling, and they appear to impair the brain's reward circuitry — the system that makes activities feel pleasurable or worthwhile.

"I don't think that this is likely important for everyone with depression," Dr. Goldsmith said. "But inflammation may help explain why a lot of individuals don't respond to first-line treatments for depression."

A recent clinical trial tested a rheumatoid arthritis medication — designed specifically to reduce inflammation — in 30 adults with depression and elevated inflammatory markers. Participants taking the drug experienced modest improvements, particularly in the physical symptoms of depression like fatigue and sluggishness. While the results did not reach statistical significance, researchers described the trial as a "proof of concept" warranting larger studies.

Why South Asians Should Pay Attention

This is where the story intersects directly with diaspora health.

South Asians carry a well-documented predisposition to metabolic syndrome — the cluster of conditions that includes insulin resistance, visceral fat accumulation, elevated triglycerides, and chronic low-grade inflammation. The landmark MASALA (Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America) study, led by researchers at Northwestern University, has shown that South Asians develop these metabolic risk factors at lower BMIs, younger ages, and higher rates than virtually any other ethnic group.

Chronic low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of metabolic syndrome. Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) — the same inflammatory markers now being linked to treatment-resistant depression — are commonly elevated in South Asian populations, even in individuals who appear outwardly healthy.

This creates a troubling possibility: a meaningful subset of depressed NRIs may be experiencing inflamed depression without knowing it, and their standard antidepressant prescriptions may be working against the wrong mechanism entirely.

The Stigma Compound

Mental health stigma in South Asian communities adds another layer of complexity. Depression is already underdiagnosed and undertreated in the diaspora — many families frame persistent fatigue, withdrawal, and loss of motivation as laziness, weakness, or simply the cost of working hard abroad. When a patient does seek help and is prescribed an SSRI that fails to improve their symptoms, the experience can reinforce the cultural narrative that depression is not a "real" medical condition.

The emerging understanding of inflamed depression offers a potential corrective. If a blood test can identify elevated inflammatory markers and predict which patients are unlikely to respond to standard antidepressants, it transforms depression from a vague mood disorder into something measurably biological — with a targeted treatment pathway.

Several research groups, including teams at Emory and the University of Cambridge, are now developing protocols to screen depression patients for inflammatory biomarkers before prescribing medication, though these are not yet in routine clinical use.

What You Can Do Now

While anti-inflammatory drugs for depression remain experimental, the underlying biology points to familiar lifestyle interventions that are already supported by strong evidence:

Anti-inflammatory diets rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fatty fish, and traditional Indian spices like turmeric, ginger, and black pepper have been shown to reduce CRP and IL-6 levels. A recent JAMA study found that an anti-inflammatory eating pattern reduced dementia risk by up to 29%, even in people with Alzheimer's biomarkers.

Regular exercise — particularly 90 to 120 minutes of strength training per week, as a recent meta-analysis in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine* suggested — is one of the most potent anti-inflammatory interventions available, with effects that rival some medications.

Sleep quality matters as well. Chronic sleep deprivation elevates inflammatory markers and suppresses immune function. Adults sleeping fewer than six hours per night have been shown to be three to four times more likely to develop infections after viral exposure.

For NRIs experiencing persistent, treatment-resistant depressive symptoms — especially fatigue, brain fog, and physical heaviness — asking a physician to check inflammatory markers like CRP is a reasonable and increasingly supported step. It costs little, it risks nothing, and it may redirect treatment toward a more effective approach.

The takeaway is not that SSRIs are wrong for everyone — they remain effective for millions. But for the subset of patients whose depression is fuelled by inflammation, a different conversation is overdue.

*Reporting based on research from Emory University School of Medicine, the University of Cambridge, the MASALA Study (Northwestern University), and clinical coverage by The New York Times.*
